caption:
Anthropic has reported to South Korea's privacy regulator that account details of about 100 Korean business customers of Claude were exposed.
The security startup Cathedral reached names, emails and plan details through outside business software, an Anthropic staffer said.
Anthropic says prompts, outputs and payment data were not accessed.

paragraphs.text: Anthropic has reported to South Korea's Personal Information Protection Commission that account information belonging to about 100 Korean enterprise customers of its Claude service was exposed, according to the Korean newspapers Hankook Ilbo and Kyunghyang Shinmun. The company filed the report on October 31, 2026, and the commission confirmed on November 9 that it had received it.

The exposure is linked to Cathedral, a US security startup that reached Anthropic's internal business systems through a vulnerability in third party business software. The Washington Post first reported that access on October 26, 2026, according to both Korean outlets.

Lydia Hallie, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, wrote on X that Cathedral accessed account information such as names, email addresses and plan details without authorization. She said prompts, model outputs and payment information were not accessed, according to Kyunghyang Shinmun and Data Studios.

A notice that Anthropic sent to some business customers lists a wider set of items that may have been exposed. According to Kyunghyang Shinmun and Hankook Ilbo, it names account and organization identifiers, names and email addresses, work contact details, and usage and spending amounts. Data Studios noted that the spending detail appears in secondary summaries of the notice and has not been confirmed in Anthropic's public statements.

RuntimeWire, which based its account on a thread by security researcher Jamieson O'Reilly quoting the customer email, reported on November 7 that the notice did not name the security firm and said Anthropic could not confirm whose information had been viewed, while telling recipients they faced no heightened risk.
Anthropic's response and the regulator's review

Anthropic said it blocked the affected systems on the day it learned of the incident and worked with the software vendor to close the vulnerability, Hankook Ilbo reported. When the incident first became public in October, the company described the access as limited to a set of sales, human resources and IT platforms that run on third party software, according to Data Studios.

The Personal Information Protection Commission said it is reviewing the report but has not yet opened a formal investigation. For companies based outside Korea, the commission may first request documents before starting a probe, which can add time, and it said it would examine the scale of the damage once a formal investigation begins, according to both newspapers.

Anthropic and Cathedral disagree about whether the access counted as authorized security research under Anthropic's vulnerability disclosure program, Data Studios reported. Anthropic has not published a global count of affected accounts, and it is not yet known which other regulators were notified.

The exposed data does not include the content of conversations with Claude, which is what most business customers worry about first. Contact details combined with plan and account identifiers can still be useful to attackers writing convincing phishing messages, so the practical risk for affected companies lies in fake billing or account requests that look authentic. The case also shows that an AI company's exposure often runs through the ordinary office software it uses rather than through its models.
Watch whether Korea's Personal Information Protection Commission opens a formal investigation, and whether Anthropic discloses how many customers outside Korea received the same notice.
